source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition
finding: People predicted total duration or extent of everyday events from one observed value. Median answers matched Bayesian predictions built from real-world priors in 5 of 8 analysable domains. Gaussian, power-law and Erlang priors gave different curve shapes, as predicted.
numbers: Two groups of undergraduates, 208 and 142. Analysed responses: movie grosses 174, poems 197, lifespans 197, pharaohs 191, movie run times 136, US House terms 130, cake baking 126, waiting times 158. No parameters tuned for the 5 empirical-prior domains.
quote: People's judgments for life spans, movie run times, movie grosses, poem lengths, and terms of U.S. representatives were indistinguishable from optimal Bayesian predictions
limits: Only group medians were tested. Marriage data dropped because 52% answered 'forever'. No test of individual-level behaviour. Fit judged by eye against bootstrap bars.
agent_relevance: The strong claim (people hold accurate priors) rests on aggregate data. Treat 'matches the prior' as a population statement, not proof an agent or person reasons Bayesian.

source: Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2006) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition
finding: The two clear misses show where the account is weak. Pharaoh reigns: people knew the Erlang shape but set the scale too high. Waiting times had no known true prior, so the authors fitted one to the human data.
numbers: Pharaoh follow-up: 35 undergraduates, median stated typical reign 30 years, Erlang b = 17.9 versus true about 9.34. Waiting-time power-law fit gamma = 2.43, chosen to minimise squared error to the human medians.
limits: Fitting the prior to the behaviour it is meant to explain is circular for waiting times (a free-prior degree of freedom). Pharaoh error was explained post hoc by analogy to modern monarchs.
agent_relevance: Where the prior is unknown, fit quality says little. A scaffold that selects by prior must state where the prior came from.

source: Mozer, Pashler & Homaei (2008) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition: the wisdom of individuals or crowds?
finding: Re-analysis of the 2006 data with a rival: each person has only k=2 stored examples (Min2 model: take the smaller relevant example, else guess). Min2 fit the median data about as well as the full Bayesian model in 8 domains. Accuracy of the crowd median does not need accurate individual priors.
numbers: Min2 used guess factor g = 0.30 (g = 0.03 for lifespans); sample-prior variants used k = 1 to 5; 10,000 simulated participants per model; 100 replications for error bars. Same prior parameters as the original paper.
limits: Min2 also had one free parameter. Lifespans fit only with g lowered to 0.03. Models with more samples (k>=5) drift toward the query point in some domains.
agent_relevance: Matching a group average cannot tell a true Bayesian reasoner from a cheap heuristic. Test the individual level, not only the mean.

source: Mozer, Pashler & Homaei (2008) Optimal predictions in everyday cognition: the wisdom of individuals or crowds?
finding: Discriminating test: spread between individuals. Small-sample models predict large between-person variance and large-sample (veridical prior) models predict small. Real people were more variable than every sample model with k>1.
numbers: Variance ratio V(d) = mean log10(human variance / model variance) over 5 query points; V(d) > 0 for k > 1 in all models (human more variable). Raw data supplied by Griffiths.
limits: Humans were also more variable than the k=1 and k=2 models in some domains, which the authors attribute to rounding and a variable guess factor. Rival fits are not unique.
agent_relevance: Individual-level variance is the experiment that separates a full posterior from a few samples. It also fits the finding that single LLM samples are noisy and need aggregation.

source: Vul, Goodman, Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2014) One and done? Optimal decisions from very few samples
finding: Explains why people act on 1 or a few samples from their posterior (probability matching): when sampling costs time, deciding from very few samples maximises reward rate. This rescues the Bayesian view by turning an apparent violation into resource-rational behaviour.
numbers: For an action/sample time ratio below 10, one sample is optimal under a symmetric reward. With no punishment for errors the ratio must be 2 or more before a second sample helps. Optimal sample count is 0 or 1 for ratios below about 25 in the sequential policies. More alternatives raise the optimal number.
limits: A theory paper, not a new experiment. It accommodates data after the fact; the sampling cost is a free quantity that is rarely measured.
agent_relevance: Design rule: with cheap parallel samples a scaffold should draw several and aggregate in code; one sample per decision is only right when sampling is costly.

source: Perfors, Tenenbaum, Griffiths & Xu (2011) A tutorial introduction to Bayesian models of cognitive development
finding: Authors of the programme state its limits: optimality is a claim that needs care, human thinkers are not optimal in many ways, and the brain may only approximate Bayes. They propose rational process models as the bridge, and note these explain some but not all departures from optimality.
numbers: No new data. Section 5.1 'Optimality: what does it mean?' and a section on how a brain could approximate inference.
limits: A tutorial, so claims are conceptual rather than measured.
agent_relevance: Use Bayesian ideals as a yardstick for what a good update looks like, not as a description of what the model does.

source: Jones & Love (2011) Bayesian Fundamentalism or Enlightenment? Behavioral and Brain Sciences
finding: Main critique of the rational-only programme. Bayesian models are weakly constrained because their hypothesis sets, priors and environment assumptions are rarely measured. Many recapitulate existing mechanistic theories. Competing Bayesian models of one task are rarely compared. Proposes joining Bayesian and mechanistic levels.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers.
limits: Read as abstract from a bibliographic index, not the full article.
agent_relevance: A prior or hypothesis set chosen to fit is a hidden free parameter. Record how every prior was set.

source: Marcus & Davis (2013) How robust are probabilistic models of higher-level cognition? Psychological Science
finding: Argues the optimal-Bayes view is less promising than claimed and is undermined by post hoc practices (choice of task, response measure, prior and likelihood after seeing data). Also argues probabilistic does not equal rational or optimal.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers in the part read.
limits: Abstract only. The full paper re-analyses several published models (including the 2006 predictions study); those details were not read.
agent_relevance: Forking paths in model specification inflate fit. Fix priors and likelihood before testing.

source: Tauber, Navarro, Perfors & Steyvers (2017) Bayesian models of cognition revisited: Setting optimality aside and letting data drive psychological theory. Psychological Review
finding: Separates two ways to use a Bayesian model: as a normative optimality standard, or as a descriptive tool that instantiates a psychological theory. Three case studies show the two give different models and different conclusions. Conflating them causes confusion.
numbers: Abstract only: 3 case studies, no figures read.
limits: Abstract only.
agent_relevance: Say clearly whether a Bayesian module in the scaffold is a normative check or just a fitted description.

source: Sanborn & Chater (2016) Bayesian brains without probabilities. Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: Proposes the brain is a Bayesian sampler. With few samples it produces classic probability errors (unpacking, base-rate neglect, conjunction fallacy), so these errors need not mean non-Bayesian.
numbers: Abstract only.
limits: Abstract only. Different sampling assumptions can make nearly any error Bayesian, which is the unfalsifiability complaint.
agent_relevance: LLM errors on base rates may be sampling noise; averaging many samples can reduce them.

source: Heuristic-Anchored Bayesian Sampler study (2026) Integrating heuristics and mental sampling in belief updating
finding: A hybrid model (a heuristic gives the first estimate, samples then refine it) explained medical-diagnosis belief updating better than pure heuristic or pure Bayesian models in most conditions. People show base-rate neglect and conservatism.
numbers: New experiment N = 200 plus re-analysis of Stengard et al. 2022 data; abstract only.
limits: Abstract only; condition-level numbers not seen.
agent_relevance: Neither pure Bayes nor pure heuristics fits; mixed accounts win.

source: The myth of the Bayesian brain (2025)
finding: Recent critique: the Bayesian brain hypothesis is flexible enough to be fitted post hoc to nearly any pattern, with unclear biological plausibility and inconsistent empirical support. Contrasts with dynamic-systems and ecological accounts.
numbers: Abstract only; no numbers.
limits: Abstract only; a critical review, itself contested.
agent_relevance: Supports caution about using Bayesian as an explanation rather than a check.

source: Qiu et al. (2026, v3 of 2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Flight-recommendation task where a user's hidden preferences must be learned over 5 rounds. Off-the-shelf LLMs fall far short of an exact Bayesian assistant and mostly do not improve across rounds.
numbers: 624 simulated users, 3 interaction sets each; Bayesian assistant reaches about 80% by round 5; open models (Gemma 2, Llama 3, Qwen 2.5) plus GPT-4.1 Mini and Gemini 1.5 Pro stay far lower with little gain after round 1 (read from figure text; not every bar value parsed).
limits: Toy preference model with a uniform prior. Chain-of-thought, numeric formatting, 30 rounds and base models all failed to fix it.
agent_relevance: Never trust an LLM to carry running beliefs unaided. Keep the belief state in code and let the model fill slots (matches guardrail G5).

source: Qiu et al. (2026, v3 of 2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Fine-tuning on the Bayesian assistant's predictions (Bayesian teaching) beats fine-tuning on correct answers (oracle teaching). Tuned models agree with the Bayesian assistant about 80% of the time and transfer to unseen domains (hotel, web shopping) and to real people.
numbers: Agreement with the Bayesian assistant about 80% for Bayesian-tuned versus lower for original and oracle-tuned models. 48 human users in the human study; humans improved from round 1 to 5 (p = 0.002). Differences p < 0.001 across three base models.
limits: With real humans all models score much lower than with simulated users because human choices are inconsistent with stated preferences. Original LLMs did well at round 1 with humans because human preferences are predictable (e.g. cheaper flights), so the prior carries them.
agent_relevance: Teaching the posterior is possible by training; our scaffold cannot train, so it must compute the update in code.

source: Qiu et al. (2026, v3 of 2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Appendix finding: accuracy depends on how far the true preference is from the model's own prior. A regression of final accuracy on L2 distance from the prior mean was significant (p < 0.001) for all three Gemma variants. The elicited prior of Gemini 1.5 Pro was more diffuse than that of Gemma.
numbers: Regression coefficients significant p < 0.001; priors elicited by prompting.
limits: Elicited verbal beliefs and the prior actually used for recommending can differ; under 50% alignment between verbalised-belief predictions and direct predictions for the original models.
agent_relevance: A strong model prior helps typical cases and hurts atypical ones. Atypical problems need evidence-heavy handling.

source: Falck, Wang & Holmes (2024) Is in-context learning in large language models Bayesian? A martingale perspective
finding: Tests a necessary condition of Bayesian learning on exchangeable data: predictions should not drift with imagined future data (martingale property). Violations were found in the tested LLMs, and uncertainty did not shrink with more data at the Bayesian rate. Authors state this falsifies the claim that ICL is Bayesian.
numbers: Models: GPT-3 (2.7B and 170B), GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2-7B, Mistral-7B; three experiments on synthetic data. Mistral-7B and GPT-3-170B were closest to Bayesian; Llama-2-7B and GPT-3.5 shrank uncertainty slower and GPT-3.5 was overconfident.
limits: Small synthetic tasks, short sequences, older models; behaviour on realistic text unknown. Violation size varied by model.
agent_relevance: Do not assume repeated sampling or more context gives coherent updating. Use code-side counting for anything that must be a posterior.

source: Xie, Raghunathan, Liang & Ma (2022) An explanation of in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference
finding: In a synthetic mixture-of-concepts language (GINC), pretrained transformers and LSTMs learn from prompt examples as if inferring a hidden concept. In-context accuracy rises with more examples and longer examples, supporting the implicit-Bayes picture in a controlled setting.
numbers: Conditions that break it: one concept only gives flat curves; random transitions fail; unseen concepts fail to extrapolate. Larger models help beyond pretraining loss: 12 to 16 layers, 81% to 85% with equal validation loss 1.33. Accuracy varies widely with example order.
limits: Synthetic data and small models; theory needs distinguishability assumptions and covers in-distribution concepts only. Order sensitivity conflicts with exchangeability, as Falck et al. later test.
agent_relevance: Examples help only for tasks the model already has a prior over. Do not expect few-shot examples to teach a truly new concept.

source: Zhu & Griffiths (2024) Eliciting the priors of large language models using iterated in-context learning
finding: Chaining one model's prediction into the next prompt (iterated learning, an MCMC method) converges on the model's own prior. GPT-4 priors for causal strength, proportion estimation and everyday quantities qualitatively matched human priors, and sometimes explained GPT-4's own decisions better than a uniform prior.
numbers: Six everyday quantities from the 2006 study were re-run (lifespans, movie grosses and others); comparison by visual inspection of figures, no fit statistic. Shapes differed in places, especially pharaoh reigns.
limits: Qualitative only. The method assumes the model acts as a Bayesian learner, which Falck et al. dispute. For speculative events (superhuman AI, Mars colony) there is no ground truth.
agent_relevance: One way to read a model's prior is to sample it. Useful to see where the model's default is wrong for a task.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3. PNAS
finding: GPT-3 on 12 classic vignettes gave human-like answers on all 12 but correct on only 6. It fell for the conjunction fallacy (Linda), avoided the base-rate error in the cab problem, and treated hospital sizes as equal. Tiny changes to the text broke it.
numbers: 12 vignettes. Cab variant: 15% blue and 85% green cabs, asked about a black cab, GPT-3 said 20%. Reordering Wason options from A,K,4,7 to 4,7,A,K made it turn over A and K. In choice tasks it showed 3 of the 6 Kahneman-Tversky biases (framing, certainty, overweighting of small probabilities).
limits: GPT-3-era model; vignettes likely in training data. Authors conclude the vignette results alone do not show it reasons like a person.
agent_relevance: Correct answers on famous tasks may be recall, not Bayesian reasoning. Use fresh, perturbed items to test a belief-update step.

source: McCoy et al. (2023) Embers of autoregression: understanding LLMs through the problem they are trained to solve
finding: Behaviour tracks the prior probability of the answer text even on deterministic tasks. This is what a strong prior over strings predicts and it works against correct evidence use.
numbers: GPT-4 shift-cipher decoding 51% when the output is high-probability text, 13% when low. Word-sequence reversal 97% versus 53%. rot-13 encoding 21% for high-probability input versus 11% for low. Rare Pig Latin variant 23%. Shift-13 cipher is over 100 times more common online than shift-12.
limits: GPT-4-0613 and similar models of that period; reasoning models may differ. Tasks are string tasks, not belief updating.
agent_relevance: Selection by prior gets in the way when the right answer is unlikely. Fit to evidence must be checked by code, not by the model's sense of what looks plausible.

source: Lake, Ullman, Tenenbaum & Gershman (2017) Building machines that learn and think like people. BBS
finding: The Bayesian-programme authors argue human-like learning needs model building, causality and compositionality, not just pattern fitting, and discuss how Bayesian program learning learns characters from one example. Frames what a thinking agent still lacks.
numbers: Character-learning benchmark described there; numbers not extracted in this pass.
limits: Review with commentaries; claims about where machines fall short have partly aged with LLMs.
agent_relevance: Hypothesis-space design (compositional pieces) matters more than the update rule.

source: Griffiths (2020) Understanding human intelligence through human limitations. Trends in Cognitive Sciences
finding: Reframes the debate: Bayesian optimality is a starting point, and human behaviour is best explained by solutions to optimisation under limited time, computation and communication (resource rationality). Departures from Bayes then become predictions rather than failures.
numbers: No new data. Discusses inductive biases as priors and cultural transmission as iterated Bayesian learning.
limits: Position paper; resource-rational models add cost parameters that must themselves be measured, or they add freedom.
agent_relevance: Budget limits are part of the problem. A scaffold with fixed samples and tokens should be judged against a resource-rational yardstick.

source: Griffiths, Zhu, Grant & McCoy (2023) Bayes in the age of intelligent machines
finding: Argues Bayesian models stay useful for understanding neural networks and LLMs even though they are not mechanisms: they describe what a trained system implicitly assumes (its priors, inductive biases), at the computational level.
numbers: No new experiments; summarises studies on eliciting priors from networks and distilling priors into networks.
limits: Position paper by the programme's leading group, so it is not neutral.
agent_relevance: Bayes as a lens for inspecting an LLM's defaults rather than a claim it computes posteriors.

source: Vul, Goodman, Griffiths & Tenenbaum (2014) One and done? Optimal decisions from very few samples
finding: Sequential sampling policies (stop when evidence is strong enough) were compared with a fixed number of samples. No policy beat the others at every cost ratio, and the best fixed number stays very low when samples are expensive.
numbers: Policies tested: fixed-k, sequential probability ratio test, accumulator. Each was best at some action/sample ratio; optimal samples were 0 or 1 below ratio about 25.
limits: Simulated agents, no human data collected. Claim that few samples are rational depends on assumed costs.
agent_relevance: Adaptive stopping (sample until agreement or a check passes) has no universal winner. Pick the rule by the cost of a sample versus the cost of a wrong action.

source: Qiu et al. (2026, v3 of 2025) Bayesian teaching enables probabilistic reasoning in large language models
finding: Prompt-only fixes did not help belief updating: chain-of-thought, a numeric input format, base models, and 30 interaction rounds instead of 5 all failed to bring LLMs near the Bayesian assistant. Training on the Bayesian signal did help.
numbers: Four prompt-side variants all gave no meaningful gain (appendix C.1); fine-tuning gave about 80% agreement with the Bayesian assistant.
limits: One task family. Prompt variants limited to those the authors tried.
agent_relevance: Asking the model to reason about probabilities in text is not a fix. Put counting and normalising in code.
